title: The body and health
description: Say what hurts, and how you feel.
grammar: tener + a noun, for how you feel
grammarNote: You do not say “I have a pain”. You say tengo dolor: tener carries the feeling.

explanation.summary: Spanish says how you feel with tener followed by a noun: tengo hambre, I am hungry. It is the same pattern as the weather: the verb carries the meaning and the noun says what kind.

sections.heading: How you feel
sections.body: Tener with a noun says what you are feeling: tengo hambre, tengo sed, tengo sueño, tengo miedo, tengo fiebre. To say you are ill, you use estar: estoy enfermo. To say someone is well, estar sano.

sections.heading: Where it hurts
sections.body: A pain is dolor, and it takes the part of the body: me duele la cabeza, me duele el estómago. The verb doler works oddly: it is the body part that is the subject, and the person who feels it uses me, te, le.

sections.heading: Saying you are unwell
sections.body: A short phrase for a doctor is estar indispuesto, and estar malo means to be unwell or to taste bad. The word for a clinic is la clínica.

examples.es: No he ido al trabajo porque estoy indispuesto.
examples.en: I have not gone to work because I am unwell.
You need to go to the clinic.

items.note: Masculine: el ojo. The plural is los ojos.
Masculine: el dolor. You say tener dolor.
It is used with estar: estoy enfermo.
It is used with estar: está sana.
Feminine: la fiebre. You say tener fiebre.

drills.meaning: I am hungry: I want to eat

drills.note: The body part is the subject of doler.
Tener sueño means to be sleepy.

drills.meaning: I am thirsty: it is very hot
